summary: Defines the SNMPv2 management information base module for managing IP and ICMP implementations. Network tools use its objects to read statistics and settings from a device. It was replaced by RFC 4293.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a dashboard of gauges for the part of a computer that sends and receives internet packets. A manager can read the dials remotely.

questions: snmp mib for ip and icmp
subtitle: Management objects for monitoring IP and ICMP behavior on a device.

tldr.problem: Network managers need a standardized way to read statistics and settings about how a device's IP and ICMP implementations are working, without asking the vendor for proprietary tools.
tldr.mechanism: Defines SNMPv2 management objects for IP forwarding decisions, default TTL, address tables, datagram reassembly, fragmentation, and ICMP message counts (echoes, errors, timeouts, etc.), grouped by inbound and outbound traffic.
tldr.outcome: A management station can query these objects remotely via SNMP to monitor how packets flow through a router or host, but this specification was replaced by RFC 4293 to support both IPv4 and IPv6.

facts.label: ICMP types
facts.value: Unreachable, Time Exceeded, Quench, Redirect, Echo, Timestamp, Address Mask

today: RFC 2011 is an Internet Standard but is obsoleted by RFC 4293, which extends the MIB to support both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. The conceptual structure remains similar, but RFC 4293 handles the larger address space and new IPv6-specific fields.

sections.title: Management of IP and ICMP
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol (IP) and the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) are the core of packet routing and diagnostics on the Internet. A network manager needs to know how many packets have arrived, how many had errors, how many were forwarded, and how long fragmented packets have been waiting to be reassembled.

This MIB module defines a set of objects that a device (router, host, or terminal server) can expose to a management station. The management station runs SNMP and reads these objects to learn about the device's IP behavior. The objects are organized into two groups: IP (for datagram routing, addressing, and reassembly) and ICMP (for error and diagnostic messages).
sections.plainLanguage: Every Internet-connected device needs to send and receive packets. This lists all the counters and switches that a manager should be able to peek at to see how well that is working.

sections.title: IP Group Objects
sections.content:
The IP group contains basic scalar objects and two tables. The scalar objects are:

  • ipForwarding: whether the device is acting as a router (forwarding packets not addressed to itself).
  • ipDefaultTTL: the Time-To-Live value to use when the device originates a packet.

Counters track incoming datagrams (ipInReceives, ipInHdrErrors for bad headers, ipInAddrErrors for invalid destination addresses, ipInUnknownProtos for unsupported protocols, ipInDiscards for dropped packets). Outgoing counters (ipOutRequests, ipOutDiscards, ipOutNoRoutes) track packets the local application layer gave to IP for transmission.

The ipAddrTable lists each IP address the device has, along with its subnet mask, broadcast address, and the maximum size of a reassembled datagram on the interface that address uses.

The ipNetToMediaTable maps IP addresses to physical (MAC) addresses, used by the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP). It records whether each mapping was learned dynamically or configured statically.
sections.plainLanguage: The IP section has a few on-off switches (like whether to forward), lots of counters (packets in, packets out, errors), a list of addresses the device owns, and a table of IP-to-physical-address mappings.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Reassembly
sections.content:
When a packet is too large for the next network hop, IP fragments it into smaller pieces and attaches a fragment offset and identifier so the receiving host can reassemble them. This section of the MIB tracks the health of that process.

Reassembly: ipReasmTimeout is the number of seconds a host will hold fragments before giving up (typically 30 to 60 seconds). ipReasmReqds counts how many fragments have arrived that need reassembling. ipReasmOKs counts successful reassemblies, and ipReasmFails counts failures (due to timeout, errors, or other reasons).

Fragmentation: ipFragOKs counts datagrams that were successfully broken into fragments. ipFragFails counts packets that needed fragmenting but could not be (for example, because the Don't Fragment flag was set). ipFragCreates counts the total number of fragments created.

A manager can use these counters to detect when a network path has a bottleneck: a rise in ipReasmFails or ipFragFails indicates that MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) mismatches or MTU discovery failures are occurring.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message is too big, it gets chopped into pieces and put back together at the other end. These counters show how many times that worked, failed, or timed out waiting.

sections.title: ICMP Group: Errors and Diagnostics
sections.content:
ICMP is used to report errors and diagnostic information. The ICMP group has separate counters for each type of ICMP message, split into incoming and outgoing.

Inbound: icmpInMsgs and icmpInErrors (bad checksums, length errors), then specific message types: icmpInDestUnreachs (destination unreachable), icmpInTimeExcds (TTL exceeded), icmpInParmProbs (parameter problem), icmpInSrcQuenchs (source quench, requesting the sender slow down), icmpInRedirects (telling a host to use a better route), icmpInEchos (ping requests), icmpInEchoReps (ping replies), icmpInTimestamps (timestamp requests), icmpInTimestampReps (timestamp replies), icmpInAddrMasks (address mask requests), and icmpInAddrMaskReps (address mask replies).

Outbound: icmpOutMsgs, icmpOutErrors, and parallel counters for each outbound message type.

A manager can monitor these to detect network problems: a spike in icmpInDestUnreachs may indicate a routing misconfiguration, and a high rate of icmpInTimeExcds suggests either a very long route or TTL settings that are too low.
sections.plainLanguage: ICMP is the "are you there?" and "something went wrong" protocol. These counters show how many of each type of ICMP message came in or went out.

sections.title: Compliance and Limitations
sections.content:
A device that claims to conform to this MIB must support both the IP group and the ICMP group. However, the RFC notes an important limitation at the time: the MIB supports only IPv4. IPv4 addresses are 32-bit values, represented as a 4-octet string. IPv6, with 128-bit addresses, is not covered. Later RFCs extended the MIB framework to support both versions.

The objects are defined using SNMPv2 syntax (RFC 1902) and can be accessed via SNMPv2 or SNMPv1 (with a translation). All counter objects are 32-bit unsigned integers, which means they can overflow after reaching 4 billion; a manager reading these over time must watch for wraparound.
sections.plainLanguage: All devices that manage IP should support these counters. But this version only works for the older 32-bit IP addresses, not the newer 128-bit ones.
